value.overview: The Ring-billed Gull (Larus delawarensis) is a medium-sized gull of North America. It breeds mainly in Canada and the northern United States and spends the nonbreeding season across much of the United States, Mexico, and parts of Central America. It is adaptable and commonly uses beaches, estuaries, lakes, reservoirs, rivers, agricultural fields, landfills, parking areas, and urban waterfronts. Costa Rica lies near the southern edge of its regular wintering range, where it occurs as a migrant and nonbreeding visitor.
value.classification: The Ring-billed Gull belongs to the gull family Laridae and the genus Larus. Its scientific name is Larus delawarensis.
value.identification: Adults have a white head and underparts, pale gray back and wings, black wingtips, yellow eyes, and a yellow bill marked by a distinct black ring near the tip. The legs are yellowish or greenish yellow. It is smaller and more compact than many large Larus gulls. Juveniles and immature birds are brown and mottled, with darker bills and varying amounts of gray and white as they mature. The black bill ring is the key adult feature.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds from Alaska and western Canada across much of Canada and in parts of the northern United States. During the nonbreeding season it occurs widely in the United States and Mexico, with smaller numbers reaching Central America. In Costa Rica, it is a nonbreeding migrant recorded mainly at coastal sites, beaches, estuaries, bays, ports, lagoons, and other open-water habitats; it may also occur at inland lakes or reservoirs. It is generally less numerous than resident or more regular tropical gulls.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds reaching Costa Rica are nonbreeding visitors, usually present during the northern fall and winter and departing toward the breeding range in spring; it does not regularly breed there.
value.breeding: Ring-billed Gulls usually breed colonially on islands, shorelines, sandbars, rocky sites, and other open ground near water. The nest is a shallow scrape lined with vegetation and debris. Both adults defend the territory and share incubation and care of the young. Clutches commonly contain two or three eggs. Chicks are covered in down, leave the nest soon after hatching, and are fed and guarded by both parents until they become independent.
value.dietFeeding: This opportunistic omnivore eats fish, insects, earthworms, crustaceans, small rodents, eggs, carrion, grains, refuse, and food discarded by people. It often feeds by walking on beaches or fields, picking items from the ground, probing wet soil, scavenging around fishing areas and landfills, and catching prey in shallow water. It may also follow farm machinery or gather around human settlements where food is readily available.
value.behavior: Ring-billed Gulls are social and commonly gather in flocks, especially at feeding and roosting sites. They are strong fliers and may travel considerable distances between feeding areas and communal roosts. Adults defend breeding territories with calls, postures, and physical attacks. Outside the breeding season they are usually less territorial, although disputes over food can be vigorous. In Costa Rica, observers may find them resting or feeding among other gulls and shorebirds.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is large, and the species has generally increased or remained stable over much of its range, although local populations may vary.
